synopsis: Across the synthesis, planning chapter, skeptic’s review and glossary, Directive (EU) 2024/2853 is stated to apply to products placed on the market after 9 December 2026; the skeptic’s review also includes products put into service and explicitly includes software updates as products [f51, f9802, f10676, f10678, f12422]. Courts may order disclosure of evidence, and defectiveness may be presumed when evidence is withheld or technical complexity makes proof excessively difficult, making simulation records, assumptions and gaps potential claimant evidence [f10679, f10680, f12201, f12434]. The proposed braking function’s regulatory route remains unconfirmed, no universal rule on virtual testing’s sufficiency for this off-road product was found, and machinery-specific simulation-admissibility case law was not found; the reviewer therefore identifies no legal safe harbor for simulation [f10499, f10672, f10674, f12426]. Planning should identify records retained for disclosure, assess liability if virtual evidence is challenged, obtain counsel’s opinion, and document credible, reproducible simulation and its validity limits rather than justify reduced physical testing by schedule pressure [f10237, f10278, f10675, f10683, f12426]. The on-road Benavides v. Tesla verdict of 1 August 2025 assigned Tesla 33 percent responsibility and awarded about $243 million, including $200 million punitive damages; the cited design theories concerned operating-domain restrictions and driver attention, informing recommendations to enforce and log the domain and retain event data rather than establishing an off-road ruling [f10685, f10687, f12429, f10690]. A 2015 warning about machine-function integration without OEM approval supports obtaining written brake-interface approvals, while the reviewer warns that final-stage legal sign-off is too late and liability review may reject the safety case [f10692, f12430, f12432, f10787].
